headline: Passive investing amplifies momentum, allowing stocks to stay overpriced 6-12 months after index inclusion; best active opportunities are where forced buying exhausts itself or ahead of index adds in $300-500M cap names
reasoning: James Sioud explains that passive investing mechanically magnifies momentum: once a stock is added to indices, market participants are forced to buy it regardless of fundamentals, which can keep it expensive for 6 to 12 months. Unlike a decade ago, shorting an overpriced stock immediately at the point of inclusion is more dangerous because the momentum can run much longer. Instead, the best short ideas are where that forced-buying cycle has ended and the stock begins falling. On the long side, identifying companies in the $300-500 million market cap range where a fundamental thesis coincides with an upcoming index addition allows early entry before forced flows inflate the price.
quote: I think you just have to be honest with how passive investing works and it it's essentially a magnification of momentum. If a stock is going up, it tends to continue going up, especially when it gets added to indices. So a stock can easily get overpriced on fundamentals and stay that way for 612 months as it gets added. So various indices and as many market participants are forced to buy that company. Now maybe 10 years ago, you would short that company as it gets 10% or 30% too expensive. I think these days you have to be aware that this can run a lot longer and you have to be open to riding a momentum, but also being conscious that it will break eventually. So some of the best ideas we have are where that force buy in has run out and that stock's going to start falling. But also on the flip side, identifying companies around that 300 to $500 million market cap range where we form a fundamental view that can coincide side with an index add and allow us to get earlier in that journey before it gets too expensive and ultimately take advantage of that those forced flows in the market.
episode_title: Why James says the 10-year yield matters more than another rate hike

headline: Cautious on housing-exposed sectors: AI build pulling electricians from residential construction, constraining supply even as demand falls on high prices, creating long-term structural issues but not a diabolical bear market
reasoning: James identifies a labour-market transmission mechanism between AI data centre construction and the residential housing sector. High-paying data centre jobs are drawing electricians away from residential builds, constraining housing supply just as demand weakens due to high prices. He expects both house prices and supply to fall, with supply constraints putting a floor under the price decline but creating a longer-term structural problem. The fund is cautious on housing-exposed names but does not expect a catastrophic bear market.
quote: Part of our analysis on the AI space has LED us to observe the almost magnet effect of the AI construction industry suck in labour from other parts of the market. So what we've observed is electricians being drawn to very high salaries and very high demand in data centre builds... if it's harder to find a sparky to build a house, costs are going to go up, supplies going to be constrained. Now that's coming at the same time as demand is falling due to prices. So what we kind of expect over the the next few years is both fall in house prices but also fall in supply, which will in some ways put a floor on the floor in a floor on the fall in share in house prices, but create more of a structural issue in the long term.

headline: 10-year yields rocketing from 4% to 5% matter far more than another rate hike — this is the most important price in global markets and the real risk to equity valuations
reasoning: James argues that short-term rate hike fears are already largely priced in, and that equity markets historically bottom before the last hike. The far more significant concern is the surge in 10-year bond yields from 4% to 5%, which is the rate used to build DCFs and price risk across global markets. He expects this, combined with AI-sector turmoil, to drive sector rotation rather than broad market weakness.
quote: Look, I think everybody is focused on short term bond yields and interest rates, which I think quite frankly are almost completely in the price at the moment. Equity markets tend to bottom before the last hike. You can make a pretty good argument that this is the last hike coming up. Maybe there'll be another one, but this is a historically a good time to get exposure to interest rate exposed sectors. So I'm not bearish on that part of the market. What is worrying me though is 10 year yields. They've rocketed from 4% to 5%. That's the, that's by far the more important metric. That's what we price risk on. That's how you build a DCF. That's the most important price in global equity markets or global markets more broadly.
